entries: From Early New High German reumen, a Central German umlaut variant of the regular form raumen, from Middle High German rūmen, from Old High German rūmen, from Proto-West Germanic *rūmijan, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną. By surface analysis, Raum + -en. Raumen was in use in Upper German regions up until the 17th century and is still present in dialects, compare Bavarian rama.
senses: to clear an area of debris, snow, mines, or other impediments
to evacuate, to clear an area of people
to put, to move something to a place deemed more fitting (especially of sets consisting of multiple individual items, or unwieldy large items)

entries: Literally, “around that turn”. Dreh is here probably used in the regional (East Central and Low German) sense “turn of a road, bend in a path”. Compare synonymous die Ecke (literally “that corner”).
From Middle High German wazzerstrāze. Equivalent to Wasser + Straße.

From Middle Low German wēmōt, perhaps a backformation from wēmōdich, whence German wehmütig. Analysable as Weh (“woe”) + Mut (“mood, emotional state”). The feminine under influence of the rhyming word Demut (“humbleness”, from Middle High German demüete) or other feminines ending with -mut (like Großmut, Schwermut). From Middle Low German also continental Scandinavian vemod. Dutch weemoed is native but semantically influenced by the German.
senses: melancholia, nostalgia, wistfulness (yearning for the past, homesickness)

entries: From Middle High German zenen, zennen, zenden, from Old High German zenen, zennen, zenden, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþijan. Cognate with Middle Low German tēnen, English teethe.
